intro:
Use it to show how two measured quantities relate: spend and revenue, dose and response. Each row of `data` is a point, placed by the number at `xDataKey` and the number at a `ScatterChart.Points` `dataKey`.

The grid, the axes, the legend and the readout are separate parts, so a chart has only the ones you write.

Neither axis starts at zero, because a cluster between 80 and 90 would be squeezed into a corner. `xDomain` and `yDomain` fix an axis when you need one. For categories compared by length, use a bar chart instead.

parts.Header: The strip above the plot: `title`, `value` and `caption`, with the series key or your own control on the trailing side.
parts.Grid: Lines both ways, in the theme's border colour. `rows` and `columns` are roughly how many: the axes pick round numbers near them.
parts.Points: One series, as a field of dots. Declare one per key. `sizeKey` maps a third quantity to each dot's area.
parts.Skeleton: A still field of muted dots, drawn only while `status` is `loading`.
parts.XAxis: Value labels under the plot, in round numbers.
parts.YAxis: Value labels down the side, in round numbers, with room made for them.
parts.Legend: A swatch and a name per series, over the top corner of the plot. On a chart with a header, use the header's `legend` prop instead.
parts.Tooltip: Makes the field readable by pointer and keyboard, and floats a readout beside what is being read. `showLabel={false}` keeps the reading without the readout. `hitRadius` is how far from a point the pointer still reads it. `labels` names the x key and the series in it.

examples.title: Two series
examples.description: Declare a `Points` per series. They share both axes, so the two clouds stay comparable. `color` names one of the theme's roles, and the header's `legend` prop says which is which.

examples.title: A third quantity
examples.description: `sizeKey` sizes each dot by another key. Values are spaced by the dot's area, because doubling a radius quadruples the ink. `sizeRange` sets the radius of the lowest and highest values, so sizes compare rows without giving their exact ratio. Lower `opacity` when large dots overlap. For a handful of named things, use a bubble chart.

examples.title: Loading, then data
examples.description: Add `ScatterChart.Skeleton` and drive `status`. The placeholder dots stay still, because a shimmer would read as the points moving. The real points grow in where they belong when it turns `ready`.

examples.title: Changing data
examples.description: When `data` changes, the points and both axes move to their new values over `domainDuration`, and a point keeps its identity through its series and row. A `ref` on the chart has `replay()`, which grows the points in again.

notes:
### Sizing

The chart fills its container's width and takes its height from `aspectRatio`, which applies to the plot alone, so a header does not shrink it. The default of `1` suits a scatter plot, and a wide frame flattens a cloud into a band. The plot draws in the browser after it has been measured, and the space is reserved until then, so it is not in server-rendered HTML.

### Bundle size

The chart adds about 60 KB of gzipped JavaScript to a page that uses it. A page that does not import it pays nothing, including one that imports other components from the package root.

### Colour

`color` on `ScatterChart.Points` names a role in the theme. Every series defaults to `chart-1`, so give the others their own.

### Missing values

A row with no number at `xDataKey` or at a series' `dataKey` draws no point for that series, and that series adds nothing to the axes for that row.

### Reading a point

With a `Tooltip`, the point nearest the pointer is read, as long as it is within `hitRadius`. It swells and turns solid. A click or a tap pins the reading until the next press elsewhere, or Escape. On a touch screen a sideways drag reads the points it passes, and a vertical drag scrolls the page.

`onActivePointChange` fires when the point changes, not on every frame, so it can drive a readout outside the chart, as the first example does. Inside the chart, `useScatterChart` gives the same point. `showLabel={false}` keeps all of this and hides the popover.

### Keyboard

With a `Tooltip`, the plot takes focus. The arrow keys move through the points from left to right, Home and End go to the first and last, Enter or Space pins the reading, and Escape clears it.

### Screen readers

Each row is given as text beside the drawing. `label` names the chart and `labelForDatum` writes a row, for values with a unit. Without them a row is read as its x, series and size keys and values, so any other field, such as a name, needs `labelForDatum`.

### Reduced motion

With reduced motion set, the points and the axes appear at their final values, without the entrance.
propsNote: `ScatterChart`, `ScatterChart.Header` and `ScatterChart.Legend` also take the props of the element they render, and a `className`. `ScatterChart.Tooltip` puts its `className` on the readout. The other parts draw nothing themselves and take only the props listed.
